description: Hello, we are Team Valkyries of Venus. Our team consists of curious physics students who want to improve their skills throughout the creative process. We aim to combine our physics knowledge with creativity to tackle challenges related to space and Earth. If you are like us, we would love to have you on our team!
summary:
Understanding abstract concepts as a young child is not very easy. Curiosity about topics such as how time began to flow or how many dimensions might exist in the universe encourages children to think and explore. However, young and curious observers growing up on Earth, a planet where they have relatively little life experience, may struggle to establish a meaningful connection with the concept of space. Our game may not answer all of a child's questions, but it aims to provide a solid foundation that encourages them to think, explore, and find their own answers. 

As a team, we wanted to begin our game not by immediately placing the player on Mars, but by first exploring their relationship with Earth. Our aim was to help children understand how the choices they make on Earth can affect their ability to survive in space. Through these choices, we also wanted to teach them that there is no absolute right answer in science and that every decision offers an opportunity to learn a valuable lesson. 

In each scenario they encounter, players will face a problem and use the knowledge they gain to overcome it. With the confidence that comes from their accumulated experience, they will eventually be ready to take the next step and establish a new life on Mars.
details:
We named our project "Mars: Butterfly Orbit" to reflect its core purpose. In space exploration, just like the butterfly effect, even the smallest equipment choice made on Earth can drastically alter a crew's fate on Mars. Our game is designed around the cognitive abilities of children aged 7-12. Information is not given directly; instead, it is learned through hands-on experience. By learning through their own experiences, we aim for the players to become more confident in making decisions in their subsequent playthroughs. 

The game consists of three phases. The first phase begins on Earth. The astronaut's initial task is to choose the spacecraft's shielding material. This choice not only determines durability in space but also dictates the vehicle's volume, restricting the payload options the player can take. The available payload capacity allows the player to diversify their space experience with options such as data sensors, ion propulsion, a seed greenhouse, an ice drill, and sample collectors. For example, a player who selects the James Webb data sensor can experience what lies behind a cosmic dust cloud, while a player without it faces a completely different consequence. The presence or absence of equipment is intended to provide different educational lessons. 

In the second phase, our player is in space. Regardless of their chosen equipment, every player will face 3 main scenarios during their journey to Mars. However, the choices made on Earth will change the outcomes of these scenarios. First, approaching a sphere, the player will learn about a star's structure. Then, encountering a cosmic dust cloud, the player will learn what material is needed to pass through without collision damage—and if they have the right sensor, they can make observations. Players can record their findings in the "Astronaut Notebook." In the final section before reaching Mars, our player witnesses a supernova. By gathering elements emitted by the supernova, they record them in the "Element Notebook." Thanks to the notes in these two notebooks, players can identify their shortcomings and strategize for their next flight. 

The final phase is starting a life on Mars. The events experienced during the space journey have altered the player's parameters, such as energy, hull integrity, and equipment. Consequently, the player's ability to adapt to a new life is tested through the results of their previous choices. The player can grow plants, learn how to handle emergencies like radiation, and upgrade outpost structures by integrating supernova elements. After completing the survival mission, the player is presented with 3 final choices: 

  1. Return to Earth or call for help to land. 
  2. Continue their life on Mars. 
  3. Travel into a black hole. 

Players who choose to return to Earth learn what happens to human muscles in a microgravity environment and visit a physiotherapist. Players who selected the Chandra data sensor on Earth have the unique opportunity to travel to a black hole. Using Chandra to detect X-rays, players journeying to the black hole will experience the "Spaghetti effect". 

Our game does not consist of "good" or "bad" endings. The core focus is to instill an understanding of the butterfly effect and a sense of responsibility in children.

To bring this chain of choices and consequences to life, we built the game with React, TypeScript, and Vite, using SVG and CSS for interactive scenes and animations, and the Web Audio API for procedural sound effects and music. A shared mission state carries the player’s equipment, resources, discoveries, and damage throughout the journey, while game rules remain separate from scene text to support testing and Turkish–English localization. NASA archive images and a historical DONKI event provide real-world references, with OSDR and Veggie informing the health and plant-growing sections. Automated rule tests and Playwright browser checks helped us verify the interactions. Our team created the story, scenarios, and educational direction; OpenAI Codex assisted with implementation, debugging, text editing, and translation.
